The Abbasid Caliphate. From 750 to 1258 of the common era, it was the longest-lived Islamic dynasty, founded by the revolutionary Abbasid family and centered in Baghdad, which became the cultural and intellectual heartland of the entire Islamic world. They patronized science, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy at the legendary House of Wisdom. But their power fragmented as regional dynasties claimed independence, and ultimately the Mongol conquest ended their rule.

The Abbasids established Baghdad in 762 as the new capital—a planned city that became the largest and most cosmopolitan metropolis of the medieval world. In the ninth century, they inaugurated the House of Wisdom, where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts, preserving classical knowledge while advancing mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. Power shifted from Arab aristocrats to a Persian-influenced bureaucratic elite. They promoted non-Arabs and fostered a more inclusive Islamic identity centered on religious learning rather than Arab kinship. The dynasty produced towering intellectual figures: Al-Ghazali in philosophy and theology, Al-Razi and Ibn Sina in medicine, Al-Khwarizmi in mathematics and algorithms. Gradually, though, they lost territorial control as regional dynasties—the Fatimids, the Seljuks, the Mamluks—carved out autonomous zones, leaving the Baghdad caliphs with symbolic rather than imperial authority by the eleventh century. Then the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258 under Hulagu Khan devastated the city and ended the caliphate, though it continued in exile in Cairo under Mamluk protection.

The Abbasids defeated the earlier Umayyad Caliphate in their revolutionary takeover. They competed against the Fatimid Caliphate, a rival Shiite caliphate challenging their legitimacy. The Turkish Seljuk Empire conquered much Abbasid territory. And the philosophers, physicians, and mathematicians they patronized—Al-Ghazali, Ibn Sina—defined an age.
